section_summary: This section completes a paper on civic participation in Japanese cities, presents a July 1949 paper on the office of mayor, and begins a paper on city assemblies. The papers compare Japanese local government with systems in the United States, Britain, and continental Europe, and argue for effective local autonomy, public accountability, and secure municipal finances.

subfiles.title: The Local Autonomy Program for the Cities of Japan, Paper No. 1 (conclusion)
subfiles.from: Headquarters Eighth United States Army, Civil Affairs Section, Legal and Government Division
subfiles.about: The concluding pages urge Japanese citizens to sign petitions thoughtfully and participate in civic organizations and city affairs.
subfiles.summary: Using cautionary stories about unread signatures, the paper warns against signing petitions casually. It describes American civic organizations and urges Japanese citizens to participate independently in local government, culture, and public life.

subfiles.title: The Local Autonomy Program for the Cities of Japan, Paper No. 2: The Office of Mayor
subfiles.from: Headquarters Eighth United States Army, Civil Affairs Section, Legal and Government Division
subfiles.about: A comparative study explains the Japanese mayor’s legal powers, relationships, and responsibilities under the Law Concerning Local Autonomy.
subfiles.summary: The paper compares German, English, and American municipal executives before examining the Japanese mayor’s eligibility, staff, administrative authority, dealings with the assembly and governor, and duties under national laws. It discusses petitions and recalls, inadequate city finances, boundary changes, and cooperation among local governments. It urges mayors to lead city planning, report clearly to residents, and work together through the Mayor’s Congress of All Japan.

subfiles.title: The Local Autonomy Program for the Cities of Japan, Paper No. 3: The Assembly in Japan
subfiles.from: Headquarters Eighth United States Army, Civil Affairs Section, Legal and Government Division
subfiles.about: The opening of Paper No. 3 argues that elected city assemblies are essential to Japanese representative government.
subfiles.summary: The paper contrasts empowered assemblies with prewar Japanese councils and authoritarian European municipal systems. It explains cities as public corporations, identifies the assembly’s authority under the Law Concerning Local Autonomy, and describes membership, officers, and committees. Comparisons with foreign cities support its proposal to reduce the size of Japanese city and prefectural assemblies.
